entries.2bb881e6af618e470907ad39477641dff9923448: <div sID="gen12937" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="121" osisID="Ps.121" sID="Ps.121"/> <div eID="gen12937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12938" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12939" type="x-p"/> Some call this the soldier's psalm, and think it was penned in the camp, when David was hazarding his life in the high places of the field, and thus trusted God to cover his head in the day of battle. Others call it the traveller's psalm (for there is nothing in it of military dangers) and think David penned it when he was going abroad, and designed it <hi type="italic">pro vehiculo—for the carriage,</hi> for a good man's convoy and companion in a journey or voyage. But we need not thus appropriate it; wherever we are, at home or abroad, we are exposed to danger more than we are aware of; and this psalm directs and encourages us to repose ourselves and our confidence in God, and by faith to put ourselves under his protection and commit ourselves to his care, which we must do, with an entire resignation and satisfaction, in singing this psalm. I. David here assures himself of help from God, <reference osisRef="Ps.121.1-Ps.121.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. He assures others of it, <reference osisRef="Ps.121.3-Ps.121.8">ver. 3-8</reference>.
entries.e381f4e14829e840acc38a8bb8574c8bd3219761: <div eID="gen12939" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12938" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Confidence in God.</title> <div sID="gen12940" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help. <hi type="super">2</hi> My help <hi type="italic">cometh</hi> from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , which made heaven and earth. 3 He will not suffer thy foot to be moved: he that keepeth thee will not slumber. <hi type="super">4</hi> Behold, he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep. <hi type="super">5</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy keeper: the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy shade upon thy right hand. 6 The sun shall not smite thee by day, nor the moon by night. <hi type="super">7</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall preserve thee from all evil: he shall preserve thy soul. <hi type="super">8</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from this time forth, and even for evermore. <div eID="gen12940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12941" type="x-p"/> This psalm teaches us, <div eID="gen12941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12942" type="x-p"/> I. To stay ourselves upon God as a God of power and a God all-sufficient for us. David did so and found the benefit of it. 1. We must not rely upon creatures, upon men and means, instruments and second causes, nor make flesh our arm: "<hi type="italic">Shall I lift up my eyes to the hills?</hi>"—so some read it. "Does my help come thence? Shall I depend upon the powers of the earth, upon the strength of the hills, upon princes and great men, who, like hills, fill the earth, and hold up their heads towards heaven? No; <hi type="italic">in vain is salvation hoped for from hills and mountains,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.3.23">Jer. iii. 23</reference>. I never expect help to come from them; my confidence is in God only." <hi type="italic">We must lift up our eyes above the hills</hi> (so some read it); we must look beyond instruments to God, who makes them that to us which they are. 2. We must see all our help laid up in God, in his power and goodness, his providence and grace; and from him we must expect it to come: "<hi type="italic">My help comes from the Lord;</hi> the help I desire is what he sends, and from him I expect it in his own way and time. If he do not help, no creature can help; if he do, no creature can hinder, can hurt." 3. We must fetch in help from God, by faith in his promises, and a due regard to all his institutions: "<hi type="italic">I will lift up my eyes to the hills</hi>" (probably he meant the hills on which the temple was built, Mount Moriah, and the holy hill of Zion, where the ark of the covenant, the oracle, and the altars were); "I will have an eye to the special presence of God in his church, and with his people (his presence by promise) and not only to his common presence." When he was at a distance he would look towards the sanctuary (<reference osisRef="Ps.28.2">Ps. xxviii. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.42.6">xlii. 6</reference>); thence <hi type="italic">comes</hi> our <hi type="italic">help,</hi> from the word and prayer, from the secret of his tabernacle. <hi type="italic">My help cometh from the Lord</hi> (so the word is, <reference osisRef="Ps.121.2">v. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">from before the Lord,</hi> or <hi type="italic">from the sight and presence of the Lord.</hi> "This (says Dr. Hammond) may refer to Christ incarnate, with whose humanity the Deity being inseparably united, God is always present with him, and, through him, with us, for whom, sitting at God's right hand, he constantly maketh intercession." Christ is called the <hi type="italic">angel of his presence,</hi> that saved his people, <reference osisRef="Isa.63.9">Isa. lxiii. 9</reference>. 4. We must encourage our confidence in God with this that he <hi type="italic">made heaven and earth,</hi> and he who did that can do any thing. He made the world out of nothing, himself alone, by a word's speaking, in a little time, and <hi type="italic">all very good,</hi> very excellent and beautiful; and therefore, how great soever our straits and difficulties are, he has power sufficient for our succour and relief. He that made heaven and earth is sovereign Lord of all the hosts of both, and can make use of them as he pleases for the help of his people, and restrain them when he pleases from hurting his people. <div eID="gen12942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12943" type="x-p"/> II. To comfort ourselves in God when our difficulties and dangers are greatest. It is here promised that if we put our trust in God, and keep in the way of our duty, we shall be safe under his protection, so that no real evil, no mere evil, shall happen to us, nor any affliction but what God sees good for us and will do us good by. 1. God himself has undertaken to be our protector: <hi type="italic">The Lord is thy keeper,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.121.5">v. 5</reference>. Whatever charge he gives his angels to keep his people, he has not thereby discharged himself, so that, whether every particular saint has an angel for his guardian or no, we are sure he has God himself for his guardian. It is infinite wisdom that contrives, and infinite power that works, the safety of those that have put themselves under God's protection. Those must needs be well kept that have <hi type="italic">the Lord</hi> for their <hi type="italic">keeper.</hi> If, by affliction, they be made his prisoners, yet still he is their keeper. 2. The same that is the protector of the church in general is engaged for the preservation of every particular believer, the same wisdom, the same power, the same promises. <hi type="italic">He that keepeth Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.121.4">v. 4</reference>) <hi type="italic">is thy keeper,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.121.5">v. 5</reference>. The shepherd of the flock is the shepherd of every sheep, and will take care that not one, even of the little ones, shall perish. 3. He is a wakeful watchful keeper: "<hi type="italic">He that keepeth Israel,</hi> that keepeth thee, O Israelite! <hi type="italic">shall neither slumber nor sleep;</hi> he never did, nor ever will, for he is never weary; he not only does not sleep, but he does not so much as slumber; he has not the least inclination to sleep." 4. He not only protects those whom he is the keeper of, but he refreshes them: He <hi type="italic">is their shade.</hi> The comparison has a great deal of gracious condescension in it; the eternal Being who is infinite substance is what he is in order that he may speak sensible comfort to his people, promises to be their <hi type="italic">umbra</hi>—their <hi type="italic">shadow,</hi> to keep as close to them as the shadow does to the body, and to shelter them from the scorching heat, as <hi type="italic">the shadow of a great rock in a weary land,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.32.2">Isa. xxxii. 2</reference>. Under this shadow they may sit with delight and assurance, <reference osisRef="Song.2.3">Cant. ii. 3</reference>. 5. He is always near to his people for their protection and refreshment, and never at a distance; he <hi type="italic">is</hi> their <hi type="italic">keeper</hi> and <hi type="italic">shade on their right hand;</hi> so that he is never far to seek. The right hand is the working hand; let them but turn themselves dexterously to their duty, and they shall find God ready to them, to assist them and give them success, <reference osisRef="Ps.16.8">Ps. xvi. 8</reference>. 6. He is not only at their right hand, but he will also <hi type="italic">keep the feet of his saints,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.9">1 Sam. ii. 9</reference>. He will have an eye upon them in their motions: <hi type="italic">He will not suffer thy foot to be moved.</hi> God will provide that his people shall not be tempted above what they are able, shall not fall into sin, though they may be very near it (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.2">Ps. lxxiii. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.73.23">23</reference>), shall not fall into trouble, though there be many endeavouring to undermine them by fraud or over throw them by force. He will keep them from being frightened, as we are when we slip or stumble and are ready to fall. 7. He will protect them from all the malignant influences of the heavenly bodies (<reference osisRef="Ps.121.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">The sun shall not smite thee</hi> with his heat <hi type="italic">by day nor the moon</hi> with her cold and moisture <hi type="italic">by night.</hi> The sun and moon are great blessings to mankind, and yet (such a sad change has sin made in the creation) even the sun and moon, though worshipped by a great part of mankind, are often instruments of hurt and distemper to human bodies; God by them often smites us; but his favour shall interpose so that they shall not damage his people. He will keep them <hi type="italic">night and day</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.3">Isa. xxvii. 3</reference>), as he kept Israel in the wilderness by <hi type="italic">a pillar of cloud by day,</hi> which screened them from the heat of the sun, <hi type="italic">and of fire by night,</hi> which probably diffused a genial warmth over the whole camp, that they might not be prejudiced by the cold and damp of the night, their father Jacob having complained (<reference osisRef="Gen.31.40">Gen. xxxi. 40</reference>) that <hi type="italic">by day the drought consumed him and the frost by night.</hi> It may be understood figuratively: "Thou shalt not be hurt either by the open assaults of thy enemies, which are as visible as the scorching beams of the sun, or by their secret treacherous attempts, which are like the insensible insinuations of the cold by night." 8. His protection will make them safe in every respect: "<hi type="italic">The Lord shall preserve thee from all evil,</hi> the evil of sin and the evil of trouble. He shall prevent the evil thou fearest, and shall sanctify, remove, or lighten, the evil thou feelest. He will keep thee from doing evil (<reference osisRef="2Cor.13.7">2 Cor. xiii. 7</reference>), and so far from suffering evil that whatever affliction happens to thee there shall be no evil in it. Even that which kills shall not hurt." 9. It is the spiritual life, especially, that God will take under his protection: <hi type="italic">He shall preserve thy soul.</hi> All souls are his; and the soul is the man, and therefore he will with a peculiar care preserve them, that they be not defiled by sin and disturbed by affliction. He will keep them by keeping us in the possession of them; and he will preserve them from perishing eternally. 10. He will keep us in all our ways: "<hi type="italic">He shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in.</hi> Thou shalt be under his protection in all thy journeys and voyages, outward-bound or homeward-bound, as he kept Israel in the wilderness, in their removes and rests. He will prosper thee in all thy affairs at home and abroad, in the beginning and in the conclusion of them. He will keep thee in life and death, thy going out and going on while thou livest and thy coming in when thou diest, going out to thy labour in the morning of thy days and coming home to thy rest when the evening of old age calls thee in," <reference osisRef="Ps.104.23">Ps. civ. 23</reference>. 11. He will continue his care over us <hi type="italic">from this time forth and even for evermore.</hi> It is a protection for life, never out of date. "He will be thy guide <hi type="italic">even unto death,</hi> and will then hide thee in the grave, hide thee in heaven. He will <hi type="italic">preserve thee in his heavenly kingdom.</hi>" God will protect his church and his saints always, <hi type="italic">even to the end of the world.</hi> The Spirit, who is their preserver and comforter, shall abide with them for ever.  <chapter eID="Ps.121"/> <div eID="gen12943" type="x-p"/>

entries.666392d404a3e90ad79d56f8ebf020477b290bf7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6985"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 121</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.121.1-Ps.121.8">Psa 121:1-8</reference>. God's guardian care of His people celebrated.</title> <div sID="gen10723" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6985"/><hi type="bold">1. I will lift up mine eyes--</hi>expresses desire (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.25.1">Psa 25:1</reference>), mingled with expectation. The last clause, read as a question, is answered, <div eID="gen10723" type="x-p"/>

entries.10123896e5a3cf596023b0fe231ab2701f672fb4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6987"/><div sID="gen10725" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6987"/>3-4. entries.e0ad40cec4fa3cd0cbca08f70734fc38cdf1bf88: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6989"/><div sID="gen10728" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6989"/>6-8. entries.9da8227f4597baa53a33fe52ea00e5a73aef7576: <div eID="gen22997" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen22998" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22999" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22999" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22998" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23000" type="x-p"/> The resolution of a godly man, <reference osisRef="Psa.121.1">Psa 121:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.121.2">Psa 121:2</reference>. The safety and prosperity of such, as they and theirs shall be under the continual protection of God, <reference osisRef="Psa.121.3-Psa.121.8">Psa 121:3-8</reference>. <div eID="gen23000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23001" type="x-p"/> This appears to be a prayer of the Jews in their captivity, who are solicitous for their restoration. It is in the form of a dialogue. <reference osisRef="Psa.121.1">Psa 121:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.121.2">Psa 121:2</reference>. The person who worships God speaks the two first verses, "I will lift up mine eyes-my help cometh," - <reference osisRef="Psa.121.1">Psa 121:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.121.2">Psa 121:2</reference>. <reference osisRef="Psa.121.3">Psa 121:3</reference>. The ministering priest answers him, "He will not suffer thy foot to be moved." "He that keepeth thee will not slumber," <reference osisRef="Psa.121.3">Psa 121:3</reference>. <div eID="gen23001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23002" type="x-p"/> To which the worshipper answers, that he knows that "he who keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep," <reference osisRef="Psa.121.4">Psa 121:4</reference>; but he seems to express a doubt whether he shall be an object of the Divine attention. <reference osisRef="Psa.121.5">Psa 121:5</reference> etc. The priest resumes; and, to the conclusion of the Psalm, gives him the most positive assurances of God's favor and protection. <div eID="gen23002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23003" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen23003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23004" type="x-p"/> Unto the hills - Jerusalem was built upon a mountain; and Judea was a mountainous country; and the Jews, in their several dispersions, turned towards Jerusalem when they offered up their prayers to God.
entries.a61c4966bbac5449e2e1624a5d61ee7058afc030: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen23004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23005" type="x-p"/> My help cometh from the Lord - There is no help for me but in my God; and I expect it from no other quarter.
entries.11e7a8a68183e65ca3e848bdb8a1ae3a1423ebf2: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen23005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23006" type="x-p"/> He will not suffer thy foot to be moved - The foundation, God's infinite power and goodness, on which thou standest, cannot be moved; and whilst thou standest on this basis, thy foot cannot be moved.
entries.7f21a78be49c61b683083916a4a93fd63ef25706: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen23006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23007" type="x-p"/> He that keepeth Israel - The Divine Being represents himself as a watchman, who takes care of the city and its inhabitants during the night-watches; and who is never overtaken with slumbering or sleepiness. There is a thought in the Antigone of Sophocles, that seems the counterpart of this of the psalmist, Ταν σαν, Ζευ, δυναμιν τις ανδρων Ὑπερβασια κατασχοι, Ταν ουθ' ὑπνος αἱ - ρει ποθ' ὁ παντογηρως, Ακαματοι τε θεων Μηνες; <div eID="gen23007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23008" type="x-p"/> Antig. ver. 613, Edit. Johnson. <div eID="gen23008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23009" type="x-p"/> Shall men below control great Jove above,Whose eyes by all-subduing sleep <div eID="gen23009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23010" type="x-p"/> Are never closed, as feeble mortals' are;But still their watchful vigil keep <div eID="gen23010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23011" type="x-p"/> Through the long circle of th' eternal year? <div eID="gen23011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23012" type="x-p"/> Franklin.
entries.6f979b5950a76abd83f62f3bf4cc51dfe24d5ae5: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen23012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23013" type="x-p"/> The sun shall not smite thee by day - Thus expressed by the Chaldee: "The morning spectres shall not smite thee by day, during the government of the sun; nor the nocturnal spectres by night, during the government of the moon." I believe the psalmist simply means, they shall not be injured by heat nor cold; by a sun-stroke by day, nor a frost-bite by night.
entries.ea1761064964806e1bbd95c3aeee7595aa83d8e9: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen23013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23014" type="x-p"/> The Lord shall preserve thee from all evil - Spiritual and corporeal, natural and moral. <div eID="gen23014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23015" type="x-p"/> He shall preserve thy soul - Take care of thy life, and take care of thy soul.
entries.a71d4890149e1ad7c6f6f1fb7db4c17db222aa80: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen23015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23016" type="x-p"/> Thy going out and thy coming in - Night and day - in all thy business and undertakings; and this through the whole course of thy life: for evermore.  <chapter eID="Ps.121"/> <div eID="gen23016" type="x-p"/>

entries.fb3b660f062baf76f0312c8ea357ccbf86ba466b: <div eID="gen10169" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Consolation of Divine Protection</title> <div sID="gen10170" type="x-p"/> This song of degrees is the only one that is inscribed שׁיר למעלות and not שׁיר המעלות. The lxx, Targum, and Jerome render it as in the other instances; Aquila and Symmachus, on the contrary, ᾠδὴ (ᾆσμα) εἰς τάς ἀναβάσεις, as the Midrash <hi type="italic">Sifrı̂</hi> also mystically interprets it: Song upon the steps, upon which God leads the righteous up into the other world. Those who explain המעלות of the homeward caravans or of the pilgrimages rightly regard this למעלות, occurring only once, as favouring their explanation. But the <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi> is that of the rule or standard. The most prominent distinguishing mark of <reference osisRef="Ps.121.1-Ps.121.8">Psa 121:1-8</reference> is the step-like movement of the thoughts: it is formed למּעלות, after the manner of steps. The view that we have a pilgrim song before us is opposed by the beginning, which leads one to infer a firmly limited range of vision, and therefore a fixed place of abode and far removed from his native mountains. The tetrastichic arrangement of the Psalm is unmistakeable.
entries.e75c12990fc8724e3fd66c7fe0e234c7fd29289a: <reference osisRef="Ps.121.1-Ps.121.4">Psa 121:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen10170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10171" type="x-p"/> Apollinaris renders as meaninglessly as possible: ὄμματα δενδροκόμων ὀρέων ὑπερεξετάνυσσα - with a reproduction of the misapprehended ἦρα of the lxx. The expression in fact is אשּׂא, and not נשׂאתי. And the mountains towards which the psalmist raises his eyes are not any mountains whatsoever. In Ezekiel the designation of his native land from the standpoint of the Mesopotamian plain is “the mountains of Israel.” His longing gaze is directed towards the district of these mountains, they are his <hi type="italic">ḳibla</hi>, i.e., the sight-point of his prayer, as of Daniel’s, Dan 6:11. To render “from which my help cometh” (Luther) is inadmissible. מאין is an interrogative even in <reference osisRef="Josh.2.4">Jos 2:4</reference>, where the question is an indirect one. The poet looks up to the mountains, the mountains of his native land, the holy mountains (<reference osisRef="Ps.133.3">Psa 133:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.137.1">Psa 137:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.125.2">Psa 125:2</reference>), when he longingly asks: whence will my help come? and to this question his longing desire itself returns the answer, that his help comes from no other quarter than from Jahve, the Maker of heaven and earth, from His who sits enthroned behind and upon these mountains, whose helpful power reaches to the remotest ends and corners of His creation, and with (עם) whom is help, i.e., both the willingness and the power to help, so that therefore help comes from nowhere but from (מן) Him alone. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.121.1">Psa 121:1</reference></hi> the poet has propounded a question, and in <reference osisRef="Ps.121.2">Psa 121:2</reference> replies to this question himself. In <reference osisRef="Ps.121.3">Psa 121:3</reference> and further the answering one goes on speaking to the questioner. The poet is himself become objective, and his Ego, calm in God, promises him comfort, by unfolding to him the joyful prospects contained in that hope in Jahve. The subjective אל expresses a negative in both cases with an emotional rejection of that which is absolutely impossible. The poet says to himself: He will, indeed, surely not abandon thy foot to the tottering (למּוט, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.66.9">Psa 66:9</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.55.23">Psa 55:23</reference>), thy Keeper will surely not slumber; and then confirms the assertion that this shall not come to pass by heightening the expression in accordance with the step-like character of the Psalm: Behold the Keeper of Israel slumbereth not and sleepeth not, i.e., He does not fall into slumber from weariness, and His life is not an alternate waking and sleeping. The eyes of His providence are ever open over Israel.
entries.cddb7543c1bc8680c6b59a15c4a16a51fd751e30: <reference osisRef="Ps.121.5-Ps.121.8">Psa 121:5-8</reference> <div eID="gen10171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10172" type="x-p"/> That which holds good of “the Keeper of Israel” the poet applies believingly to himself, the individual among God’s people, in <reference osisRef="Ps.121.5">Psa 121:5</reference> after Gen 28:15. Jahve is his Keeper, He is his shade upon his right hand (היּמין as in Jdg 20:16; <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.9">2Sa 20:9</reference>, and frequently; the construct state instead of an apposition, cf. e.g., Arab. <hi type="italic">jânbu</hi> <hi type="italic">'l - grbı̂yi</hi>, the side of the western = the western side), which protecting him and keeping him fresh and cool, covers him from the sun’s burning heat. על, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.109.6">Psa 109:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.110.5">Psa 110:5</reference>, with the idea of an overshadowing that screens and spreads itself out over anything (cf. Num 14:9). To the figure of the shadow is appended the consolation in Psa 121:6. הכּה of the sun signifies to smite injuriously (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.10">Isa 49:10</reference>), plants, so that they wither (<reference osisRef="Ps.102.5">Psa 102:5</reference>), and the head (<reference osisRef="Jonah.4.8">Jon 4:8</reference>), so that symptoms of sun-stroke (2Ki 4:19, Judith 8:2f.) appears. The transferring of the word of the moon is not zeugmatic. Even the moon’s rays may become insupportable, may affect the eyes injuriously, and (more particularly in the equatorial regions) produce fatal inflammation of the brain.<note placement="foot">Many expositors, nevertheless, understand the destructive influence of the moon meant here of the nightly cold, which is mentioned elsewhere in the same antithesis. <reference osisRef="Gen.31.40">Gen 31:40</reference>; Jer 36:30. De Sacy observes also: <hi type="italic">On dit quelquefois d'un grand froid, comme d'un grand chaud, qu'il est brulant</hi>. The Arabs also say of snow and of cold as of fire: <hi type="italic">jaḥrik</hi>, it burns.</note> <div eID="gen10172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10173" type="x-p"/> From the hurtful influences of nature that are round about him the promise extends in <reference osisRef="Ps.121.7-Ps.121.8">Psa 121:7-8</reference> in every direction. Jahve, says the poet to himself, will keep (guard) thee against all evil, of whatever kind it may be and whencesoever it may threaten; He will keep thy soul, and therefore thy life both inwardly and outwardly; He will keep (ישׁמר־, cf. on the other hand ישׁפּט־ in <reference osisRef="Ps.9.9">Psa 9:9</reference>) thy going out and coming in, i.e., all thy business and intercourse of life (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.6">Deu 28:6</reference>, and frequently); for, as Chrysostom observes, ἐν τούτοις ὁ βίος ἅπας, ἐν εἰσόδοις καὶ ἐξόδοις, therefore: everywhere and at all times; and that from this time forth even for ever. In connection with this the thought is natural, that the life of him who stands under the so universal and unbounded protection of eternal love can suffer no injury.  <chapter eID="Ps.121"/> <div eID="gen10173" type="x-p"/>

entries.ee8da8067b71ee73c56eb27c8d2de07e8e19f859:
PSALM 121
The Psalmist, to encourage true believers confidently to trust in the aid of God, and to teach them to betake themselves to his protection, first, affirms that, to whatever quarter we turn our eyes it is impossible to find salvation anywhere else; and, in the second place, extols in lofty terms the fatherly care of God in defending his faithful ones.
Song of Degrees.
Psalm 121:1-2
1. I will lift up my eyes to the mountains, whence my help will come
Phillips, who thinks it “probable that that Psalm was written just as the Israelites were about to commence their journey to their native land,” gives this explanation of the verse: “I will l lift up eyes to the mountains, viz., Zion, Tabor, Carmel, etc.; but especially to the first, as being the place of the ark, and consequently the place to which the Israelites directed their eyes, as to a fountain of all good. There they looked for help as often as circumstances rendered expected assistance requisite, as we learn from several passages in the Psalms. See Psalm 14:7; Psalm 20:3.” In returning from Babylon, how many a longing and anxious look would the Jews east to the hills of Palestine, and with how many stirring and sacred emotions would the sight of them fill their minds!
2. My help is from Jehovah, who made heaven and earth.
 
l I will lift up my eyes to the mountains. The inspired writer, whoever he was, seems, in the opening of the Psalm, to speak in the person of an unbelieving man. As God prevents his believing people with his blessings, and meets them of his own accord, so they, on their part, immediately east their eyes directly upon him. What then is the meaning of this unsettled looking of the Prophet, who casts his eyes now on this side and now on that, as if faith directed him not to God? I answer, that the thoughts of the godly are never so stayed upon the word of God as not to be carried away at the first impulse to some allurements; and especially when dangers disquiet us, or when we are assailed with sore temptations, it is scarcely possible for us, from our being so inclined to the earth, not to be moved by the enticements presented to us, until our minds put a bridle upon themselves, and turn them back to God. The sentence, however, may be explained as if expressed in a conditional form. Whatever we may think, would the Prophet say, all the hopes which draw us away from God are vain and delusive. If we take it in this sense, he is not to be understood as relating how he reasoned with himself, or what he intended to do, but only as declaring, that those lose their pains who, disregarding God, gaze to a distance all around them, and make long and devious circuits in quest of remedies to their troubles. It is indeed certain, that in thus speaking of himself, he exhibits to us a malady with which all mankind are afflicted; but still, it will not be unsuitable to suppose, that he was prompted to speak in this manner from his own experience; for such is the inconstancy natural to us, that so soon as we are smitten with any fear, we turn our eyes in every direction, until faith, drawing us back from all these erratic wanderings, direct us exclusively to God. All the difference between believers and unbelievers in this respect is, that although all are prone to be deceived, and easily cheated by impostures, yet Satan bewitches unbelievers by his enchantments; whereas, in regard to believers, God corrects the vice of their nature, and does not permit them to persevere in going astray. The meaning of the Prophet is abundantly obvious, which is, that although all the helps of the world, even the mightiest, should offer themselves to us, yet we ought not to seek safety anywhere but in God; yea, rather, that when men shall have long wearied themselves in hunting after remedies, now in one quarter and now in another, they will at length find. from experience, that there is no assured help but in God alone. By the mountains, the Prophet means whatever is great or excellent in the world; and the lesson he teaches is, that we ought to account all such favor as nothing.
Farther, these two verses ought to be read connectedly, bringing out this sense: When I shall have lifted up my eyes to the mountains, then I will at length experience that I have fallen into a rash and unprofitable mistake, until I direct them to God alone, and keep them fixed upon him. It is at the same time to be observed, that God in this place is not in vain honored with the title of Creator of heaven and earth; it being intended hereby tacitly to rebuke the ingratitude of men, when they cannot rest contented with his power. Did they in good earnest acknowledge him as Creator, they would also be persuaded, that as he holds the whole world in his hand, and governs it as seemeth good in his sight, he is possessed of infinite power. But when, hurried away by the blind impetuosity of their passions, they have recourse to other objects besides him, they defraud him of his right and empire. In this way ought we to apply this title of God to the case in hand. The amount is, that whilst we are naturally more anxious than is needful in seeking alleviation and redress to our calamities, especially when any imminent danger threatens us, yet we act a foolish and mistaken part in running up and down through tortuous mazes: and that therefore we ought to impose a restraint upon our understandings, that they may not apply themselves to any other but God alone. Nor is the opinion of those unsuitable, who think that the Hebrew word אל, el, which we translate to, namely, to the mountains, is put for על, al, which signifies above, giving this sense, That men, however high they may look, will find no true salvation except hi God.
Psalm 121:3-5
3. He will not suffer thy foot to stumble: he who keepeth thee will not slumber. 4. Behold! he who keepeth Israel will not slumber nor sleep. 5. Jehovah is thy keeper; Jehovah is thy defence
The Hebrew word is צל, tsel, “a shadow;” and hence it has been supposed that the words, “thy shadow at thy right hand.,” are a figurative expression, referring to the protection afforded by the shade of a tree against the scorching rays of the sun, or to the custom which prevails in tropical climates especially, of keeping off the intense heat of the sun by a portable screen, such as an umbrella or parasol. The word is often put for defense in general. Compare Numbers 14:9; Isaiah 30:2; Jeremiah 48:45
on thy right hand.

<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="121" type="Psalm">
                  <ns0:head>PSAL. CXXI.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:head>A song of degrees.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:argument>
                     <ns0:p>The matter of this Psalm sufficiently sheweth, that the Psalmist was conflicting with great difficulties and oppositions, and looking hither and thither for help, as men in such cases use to do, and then turning his eyes to God and his Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vidence, and encouraging himself by Gods promises made to his people.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:argument>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> shall I lift up mine eyes to the hills? whence should my help come?</ns0:note> I Will lift up mine eyes unto the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 87. 1. & 133. 3.</ns0:note> hills <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Either to <ns0:hi>Sion</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Moriah,</ns0:hi> which are called <ns0:hi>the holy mountains, Psal.</ns0:hi> 87. 1. or rather, 2. to the hills in general, whereof there were many in the land of <ns0:hi>Canaan,</ns0:hi> and upon which the forces, which he hoped would come to his aid, might be seen at a great distance.</ns0:note> from whence cometh <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>may come,</ns0:hi> Heb. <ns0:hi>will come.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> my help.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 124. 8.</ns0:note> My help <ns0:hi>cometh</ns0:hi> from the LORD <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">From God alone, and therefore to him alone will I turn mine eyes.</ns0:note> which made heaven and earth.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 He will not suffer thy foot <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">He speaketh as it were from God to himself, but withal to the encouragement of his followers and of all good men.</ns0:note> to be moved <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">To wit, so as to fall into mischief.</ns0:note>: he that keepeth thee will not slumber <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Will not overlook nor neglect any thing which is necessary for thy preservation.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 Behold, he that keepeth Israel, shall nei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther slumber nor sleep.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 The LORD <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> thy keeper: the LORD <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> thy shade <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Both to refresh thee and keep thee from the burning heat of the Sun, as it is expressed in the next verse, and to protect thee by his power from all thine enemies; for which reason God is oft called a <ns0:hi>shadow</ns0:hi> in Scripture.</ns0:note> upon thy right hand <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Partly to uphold thy right hand, which is the chief instrument of a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ction; and partly to defend thee in that place where thine enemies oppose thee: of which see on <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 109. 6. And compare <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 16. 8. & 109. 31.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 The sun shall not smite thee <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">With excessive heat.</ns0:note> by day, nor the moon <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">With that cold and moisture which comes into the air by it and with it. Intemperate heats and colds are the two springs of many diseases. He al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ludes both to the condition of Souldiers or Travellers, who are exposed to the open air by day and by night, and also to the cloudy Pillar which defended the Israelites both by day and by night. The sence is, He shall protect thee from all evils both by day and night.</ns0:note> by night.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 The LORD shall preserve thee from all evil: he shall preserve thy soul.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 The LORD shall preserve thy going out, and thy coming in <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Shall guard and assist thee in all thy expeditions and affairs and actions either at home or abroad. So this phrase is used <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 27. 17. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 28. 6.</ns0:note>, from this time forth; and even for evermore.</ns0:p>
               </ns0:div>
